title: Owe no one anything (Romans 13:8–14)
hook: except to love one another; love is the fulfilling of the law

segments.voice: Yesterday, love without pretending, love with the mask off, and your line was overcome evil with good. Did you tell someone how glad you were for them? Day three hundred twenty-eight.

Plenty of friendships run on a quiet ledger. The friend who paid for lunch last time, so it's your turn. The neighbor who watched your dog, so you owe them one. The twenty dollars your brother still hasn't paid back. Score gets kept, often without anyone meaning to, and it feels fair. Paul has just been talking about paying what you owe: taxes to whom taxes are due, honor to whom honor is due. Pay it all, he says, settle up. And then, in the very next breath, he names the one debt you can never pay off. And he says that's the one to keep.
screen: `A LITTLE MENTAL LEDGER.` → `PAY WHAT YOU OWE.` → `THE ONE DEBT YOU CAN'T PAY OFF.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the King James Bible: "Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law." Clear every other debt. But love is the debt that stays open. You never get to say: there, I've loved you enough, we're even. An old Christian writer, Origen, put it something like this: the debt of love remains with us always, and we pay it daily and always owe it. Then Paul takes the commandments, don't commit adultery, don't kill, don't steal, don't covet, and says they're all summed up in one line from the law of Moses: love your neighbor as yourself. "Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law." Fulfilling in Greek is pleroma, fullness: love fills the law up to the brim. Jesus said much the same when he named the two great commandments. Then Paul looks at the clock. The night is far spent, he says, the day is at hand. Wake up. Cast off the works of darkness, and put on the armor of light. And he ends with a line that has a famous afterlife: "But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof." Centuries later, a restless teacher named Augustine sat weeping in a garden in Milan. He heard a child's voice nearby, singing, take up and read. He opened Paul's letters, and his eyes fell on these very lines. He wrote later that a light of peace flooded his heart. He tells the story himself, in his Confessions.
screen: `THE ONE DEBT THAT STAYS OPEN.` · `LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR AS YOURSELF.` · `PLEROMA: FILLED TO THE BRIM.` · `TAKE UP AND READ: AUGUSTINE.` · then, large: `LOVE IS THE FULFILLING OF THE LAW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pay one debt, even a small one. Settle, and breathe. Scan your life for something you owe. A book you borrowed. Five dollars. A thank-you note. A reply to a message you've been putting off. A call to someone who has always called you first. Pick one, the smallest real one, and decide when today you'll pay it. Then notice the other debt, the one that never closes. Picture someone you love and notice how much you still owe them in love, and owe it gladly. If you pray, you can give thanks for that debt. The bell holds the time.
Owe no one anything. Settle every debt, Paul says, except one: love, the debt that stays open, and that fills the law to the brim.
Your line: love fulfils the law. Today, pay that one small debt, and then do one loving thing for someone you're not keeping score with. Day three hundred twenty-eight.

screen: `DAY 328 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE WEAK AND THE STRONG.`

howItsDone: Romans 13:11–14 is a traditional reading for the first Sunday of Advent in some churches, and Christians tell Augustine's conversion story as an example of how a single verse can change a life.

trapdoor: what you thought: owe no one anything is advice about money.
what it means: pay every debt, Paul says, except love, which you owe forever, because love fulfills the whole law.
what a scholar hears: Paul sums the commandments in Leviticus 19:18, and Augustine's Confessions, book eight, tells how these verses ended his long struggle.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook drops 'most of us carry' and 'we keep score'; 'take off the clothes of darkness' corrected to the text's 'cast off the works of darkness'; cut 'a line that changed history', 'about three and a half centuries later' (date not in the cited texts), 'young' and 'one of the most influential Christians who ever lived'; trapdoor drops the year 386; practice no longer tells the listener what to feel; howItsDone 'many churches' became 'some'.

The carry 'love fulfils the law' uses the British spelling 'fulfils' (as in the index); American would be 'fulfills'. The validator does not flag it, but the index may want 'fulfills'. The script keeps the index wording as required.
Origen's saying on the debt of love (Commentary on Romans, on 13:8) is paraphrased; confirm attribution and reference.
Augustine's conversion: Milan, 386 AD, Confessions 8.12 ('tolle lege'); 'a light of peace' paraphrases his account. 'About three and a half centuries later' assumes Romans c. 57. Confirm.
Romans 13:1–7 (governing authorities) is only mentioned in passing (taxes, honor); Keeper may want a note on how churches read it.
howItsDone: Romans 13:11–14 is the epistle for Advent Sunday in the Book of Common Prayer and in the Revised Common Lectionary (Year A). Confirm.
